about: The words for encounters/long_793.json (the long years, 793 to 1066): for each card long.<card>.title, .intention, .l1 ... (its lines in order), .o.<option> (the option's label); long.news.<what> for the news a choice posts on a port's board; and art.<card id>, one line for the artist of what the card's picture shows. Facts are told in the Chronicle's flat voice ('This year ...'); people speak plainly. Quotations are short and from public-domain translations named in the cards' notes (the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle after Giles 1847 and Ingram 1823; Rimbert after Robinson 1921); the rest is our own rendering of the Latin and Old English. A draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: A Frisian skipper says the West Saxon wic at Hamwic is half open while the kings quarrel: the reeve there asks fewer questions than the one at Lundenwic.
The shut ports
For some years no English ship has been let trade on the king's shores in Gaul, and King Offa has shut his own to the king's men. A Frisian skipper back from the Thames says how it stands.
King Charles asked a daughter of Offa for his son. Offa asked a daughter of Charles for his. That is the whole quarrel, and my cargo has paid for it.
At Lundenwic the reeve looks at a Frisian and sees the Frankish king. Some days he lets you land for a gift. Some days he does not.
I have black stones aboard, cut for English hand-mills, and no English shore to land them on. Take them off me cheap.
Keep to the Rhine and the north until the kings are friends
Buy two pair of his black stones for 14 d and wait for the peace
Stand him ale and ask the way round (3 d)
A Frisian skipper on a river jetty at evening, his boat riding low with rough black quernstones, jerking his thumb toward the west; grey sky, slack sail.
The kings are friends
This year King Charles wrote to King Offa as to a brother. The merchants of each realm are to have the other king's protection, and the shores are open.
A priest read it out on the dam. True pilgrims go free. A trader who hides among them pays the toll in the proper place, like the rest of us.
Offa asked for black stones of the length he likes. Our king asks in turn that English cloaks be as long as they used to be. Two kings, and they write about querns and hems.
Offa is dead since before Lammas. The letter stands. Kings die. Tolls do not.
The black stones in your hold are worth something again.
Take an order here for black stones
Take an order here for English cloaks of the old length
Hear it out and go on as before
A priest reading a sealed letter aloud on a crowded jetty in summer sun; merchants of two peoples listening, one holding a cloak against himself to measure its length.
The king's price, set at Frankfurt: a measure of oats 1 d, of barley 2 d, of rye 3 d, of wheat 4 d. The king's own corn goes cheaper still. No man may sell dearer.
The king's measure
This year at Frankfurt the king set the price of corn and bread and made one public measure for the whole realm. The count's steward is going round the boats with the new one.
Oats a penny the measure, barley two, rye three, wheat four. Twelve wheat loaves of two pounds each for a penny. Nobody sells dearer, in plenty or in dearth.
And it is this measure, not your grandfather's basket. Put yours beside it.
Have your measure checked and marked (2 d for his trouble)
Keep the old measure. It has always been good enough
Ask him to say the whole of the king's price
A steward with a new wooden corn measure and a branding iron beside a merchant's boat, grain being poured from a sack to fill it; bright morning on the river bank.
The old pennies
The king's new pennies are heavier, with his name-sign on them, and by his order they pass in every place, town and market. A seller turns your old light pennies over in his palm.
These are the old strike. A free man who refuses the new coin pays fifteen shillings to the king. Nobody said I must take the old at its face.
By weight, then. Four of yours for three of the king's.
Or carry them up to the moneyer and let him melt them. He keeps his share too.
Let him weigh them, and take the loss
Take the old coin to the moneyer for new
Pay from the bottom of the purse and talk about the weather
Keep the old pennies for the north, where all silver goes on the scales
A market seller weighing small silver pennies on a folding balance at his stall, the merchant's open purse on the board between them; noon, a crowd behind.
A buyer for mail
Since the king's order at Herstal no mail coat may be sold out of the realm. A Dane on the next jetty asks, pleasantly, whether a Frisian boat ever carries one.
I do not ask where it comes from. I pay in silver by weight, and I pay twice what a Frank pays.
You have one aboard now. I can smell the oil on it.
The king's men search the boats at the river mouths. What they find they keep.
Sell him the mail coat after dark for 260 d
Tell him you carry wine and stones
Tell the toll man there is a Dane asking after mail
A Dane in a blue cloak sitting on a mooring post at dusk, weighing a pouch of cut silver in one hand and looking at the covered hold of a Frisian boat.
By the emperor's order merchants meet the Slavs only at the named posts. Bardowick on the Ilmenau, behind the lower Elbe, is the one a boat can come near. No arms, no mail.
The posts on the border

This winter at Thionville the emperor named the places where merchants may meet the Slavs and the Avars, from Bardowick to Lorch, and set a man of his own over each. Arms and mail are not to be carried there for sale.
Bardowick, Schezla, Magdeburg, Erfurt, Hallstadt, Forchheim, Premberg, Regensburg, Lorch. Those, and no ford between them.
A man found carrying swords or mail to sell loses all he has with him. Half to the palace. The other half is shared between the emperor's men and the one who found him.
I have not looked in your hold. I am telling you the law before I do.
Ask which of the posts a boat can reach
Buy iron tools instead of blades for the eastern trade (two crates, 40 d)
Ask the clerk who rides with him what mail is, that kings fear it so
Say the law is for men who trade east, and you trade west
A king's officer in a red cloak reading from a wax tablet on a winter quay, a cleric beside him with a satchel, frost on the mooring posts, a merchant listening with folded arms.
The finder's half

Your man saw sword hilts in the wool bales going aboard the next boat, which is bound for the Danes. By the law of Thionville, half of such a cargo is shared between the emperor's men and the one who finds it.
Wool. For the weavers at Ripa. Is there something you want to say to me?
We have lain on the same dam ten winters, your house and mine.
Go to the count's man and claim the finder's share
Say nothing. It is not your hold
Tell him quietly what you saw, and let him thank you
Two boats side by side at a jetty in early light; a porter carrying a wool bale from which a sword hilt shows; one Frisian master watching the other watch.
The hungry year

There is famine in many parts of the realm. The emperor has ordered that each man feed his own, that no one sell his corn too dear, and that no food be sold out of the empire. The priest stands at the foot of your gangplank.
The order came from Thionville with the snow. Feed your own, sell fair, and nothing that can be eaten leaves the realm.
The price was set at Noviomagus in Lent. Oats two pennies the measure, barley three, rye four, wheat six. To buy at harvest and sit on it till the price doubles has a name now: filthy gain.
You have corn aboard. I can see the sacks. There are forty at my door who can see nothing else.
You have no corn. Then bring some, and I will find the silver.
Sell two sacks of wheat at the emperor's price
Sell two sacks to the man who offers most
Give a sack at the church door
Promise him corn: six sacks within forty days
A thin priest at the foot of a gangplank with a crowd of hungry people behind him in grey winter light, the merchant above him with a hand on a grain sack.
Reric on the Wendish shore is destroyed. Its merchants trade at Sliesthorp now, under the king of the Danes, behind his new wall.
Reric is gone

This year Godfred, king of the Danes, destroyed the trading place on the Wendish shore that the Danes call Reric, put its merchants aboard his ships and set them down at Sliesthorp. He has ordered a wall from sea to sea, with one gate in it.
He burned the booths and kept the men who knew how to fill them. A king who steals merchants. I would call it flattery if I had not lost a season's honey there.
The toll that Reric paid him he will take at his own door now. One gate in the wall for carts and riders, and his man standing in it.
Dragomir of Reric owed your house a welcome. If he lives, he is on the strand at Sliesthorp with what he could carry.
Send word to Sliesthorp by this skipper, to ask after the men you knew (4 d)
Buy the last cake of Wendish wax he saved (30 d): there will be less of it this year
Mark Reric off your reckoning and say no more
A burned row of booths on a low Baltic shore, Danish ships pulling off the beach loaded with men and bundles, smoke lying flat on the water; seen from a ship standing off at evening.
A king without a kingdom

This year Eardwulf, king of the Northumbrians, driven from his kingdom and his country, came to the emperor at Noviomagus and went on from there to Rome. The emperor and the pope mean to send him home with their envoys.
He goes back with the pope's deacon and two abbots of ours. An emperor does not conquer Northumbria. He lends it a king.
I need hulls that know the crossing, and masters who do not talk. It is a good year for men who take passengers for ransom.
Hire the boat to the envoys for the crossing
Sell the escort ship's bread for the passage
Keep clear of kings in exile. They pay in promises

A tall tired man in a worn king's cloak walking down to the river landing below the palace at Noviomagus with a deacon and two abbots, a Frankish officer bargaining with a boat's master in front; windy March.
The Frisians' hundred pounds

Two hundred ships from the north lie among the Frisian islands. The Frisians have fought three times and lost three times, and the Danes have set a tribute of a hundred pounds of silver. A Dane with two men behind him is going from boat to boat.
The king of the Danes counts Frisia his own. A hundred pounds from the land, and from each hull its share. Yours is thirty pennies.
Who pays is marked, and sails where he likes this summer. Who does not is also marked.
Pay the thirty pennies
Offer him a cask of wine and let him count it for thirty
Tell him your silver is the count's before it is his king's
A Danish envoy with a notched stick and two armed men on a Frisian jetty, the sails of many ships far off across the flats; a grey bright noon.
Two hundred sails

This year a fleet of two hundred ships came from the Northmen to Frisia and laid waste all the islands off the coast. The Frisians were beaten in three fights and paid a hundred pounds of silver. A man who got away tells it.
We counted sails until the boy ran out of fingers and started on his toes. Then we stopped counting and ran.
The emperor is calling out men and boats to the Weser. He was told at Aachen. By the time an emperor is told, the cows are eaten.
On the islands they will want bread, cloth and timber, and have less silver than they had.
Keep off the Frisian coast until the fleet goes home
Take him on as a hand. He has nothing to go back to
Give him 6 d and a loaf for the road
A soaked Frisian with a bundle telling his story on a foreign quay, drawing ships in the sand with a stick while a merchant's crew stand round him; late afternoon, wind.
Godfred of the Danes is dead by his own man's hand. Hemming his nephew has sworn peace with the emperor on the Eider, twelve nobles of each people.
Godfred is dead
This year Godfred, king of the Danes, was killed by one of his own following. Hemming, his brother's son, took the kingdom and made peace with the emperor.
He said he would water his horses at Aachen. One of his own men thought otherwise. That is all I know, and more than I should say.
Twelve of ours and twelve Franks swore it on the Eider, when the frost let the roads open. Hemming keeps the peace. He also keeps the gate.
The fleet has gone home. Sliesthorp is open to a Christian boat again.
Send word ahead to Sliesthorp that wine is coming (3 d to the skipper)
Ask him who holds the toll at the gate now
Let a season pass before you trust a new king's peace
Twenty-four men in cloaks facing each other across a small grey river in thin spring sun, swords held out flat between them; a ferry and reeds in front.
The dust

A plague has killed the cattle in every province of the realm, and the army's oxen with them. It is said in the markets that men sent by the duke of Benevento scatter a dust on the fields and in the springs. A crowd on the bank has hold of a stranger.
It is flour. For the love of God, it is flour. I am a carter from the Loire.
They mean to tie him to a plank and give him to the river. Some who were taken have said they did it, with the rope already on them.
Hides are cheap this year and will be dear the next.
Speak for him: taste the flour in front of them
Keep to the boat. A stranger who speaks for a stranger makes two strangers
Buy hides while the crowd is busy: three bundles for 24 d
A crowd on a river bank at dusk holding a frightened man with a small sack, a plank and a rope ready, dead cattle lying in the field behind; a merchant's boat tied close by.
The emperor is dead
This year, five nights before the kalends of February, the emperor Charles died at Aachen and was buried the same day. Louis his son came up from Aquitaine and took the whole realm.
He was king before I was born. I never knew another. The new lord has sent men through every county to hear who was wronged.
Every grant and every freedom is to be shown again and sealed again in the new name. That is how a new king learns what he owns.
Your freedom from the toll at Dorestat was given in the old emperor's name.
Have your freedom sealed again in the new emperor's name (60 d to his clerk)
Give the count's man 12 d to remember your boat kindly
Tell the emperor's men of a toll that was taken wrongly
Say a prayer for the old man and go on
A count's man in a dark cloak telling the news on a cold February quay, men standing with their hoods off, a bell swinging in a wooden church tower behind; low white sun.
The Danes' pennies
The king of the Danes now has pennies struck at Sliesthorp. They are copied from the Dorestat penny, name and all, with a ship or a stag where the letters ran out. A buyer counts some into your hand.
Count them or weigh them, as you like. Here they count. Past the gate they go on the scales like anything else.
The letters say Carolus and Dorestat. Our moneyer cannot read. Neither can I. It is good silver.
Take them by count, as he offers
Have every one on the scales
Ask for cut silver instead, as your father took it
A Dane's open hand holding small silver pennies stamped with a ship, beside a Frisian's folding scales on a plank table; the harbour palisade behind, grey noon.
Danes have plundered Dorestat, coming on it by Traiectum. Part of it is burned, and many are killed or carried off.
Dorestat has burned

This year a fleet of the Danes came into Frisia and laid waste a part of it. From there they came by Traiectum to the trading place called Dorestat and plundered everything. Some of the people they killed, some they carried off, and part of the place they burned.
They came by Traiectum, by the back water from the north, not up the Lek from the sea. Nobody watches that side. Why would they?
The emperor was busy with his sons. The count was with the emperor. The toll man hid in a wine cask, which is the first use I ever knew him make of one.
They say the swords in the Danes' hands were good Frankish work. You know how such blades go north.
Your own house stands on that bank.
Send 40 d home by a sure hand, toward the ransom of those taken
Buy what he carried out of the fire: two bolts of Frisian cloth for 50 d
Feed him, hear him out, and ask who is alive
The long row of jetties at Dorestat seen from the river at dawn, storehouses burning at one end, longships drawn up among the merchant boats, people running along the dam.
Dorestat, again
This year the Northmen laid waste Dorestat a second time. The emperor was very angry, and ordered the coasts to be guarded.
Same men, same season, same jetties. They know the way now. A raider is a merchant who has found a market with no toll.
The emperor is angry. He was angry last year, too.
Your forty pennies bought my sister back off the ships last summer. I had not forgotten it.
Have your stores carried up to Traiectum, inside the old walls (30 d)
Leave things as they are. The emperor has ordered the coast guarded
Pay a man to watch the river mouth for your house (10 d)
A Frisian skipper at an alehouse bench counting off raids on two fingers, behind him through the door a river with half-rebuilt jetties; rain.
Witla and Andoverpis
This year the Northmen burned Andoverpis on the Scheldt and the trading place of Witla at the mouth of the Maas, and came to Dorestat a third time.
Witla was forty houses and a beach. Now it is a beach. I have piloted that bar since I could stand, and there is nothing behind it to pilot anyone to.
I know the Maas mouth and the channels through to the Scheldt. I will work for bread and a place by the fire.
Your stores lay safe at Traiectum this year. Those who left theirs on the dams are selling their tools to eat.
Your stores were on the dam at Dorestat. What the fire left, the neighbours have had.
Take the pilot on
Sell from your saved stores to the burned-out, at a fair price
Send to have the ashes of your own store searched
Give him bread and wish him a harbour
A bare beach at the Maas mouth with black house posts and one boat-shed frame standing, an old pilot with a sounding pole looking at it; flat evening light, gulls.
The tribute

This year the Northmen fell on Walichrum, killed Count Eggihard and Hemming, Halfdan's son, with many others, and took tribute. From Dorestat they took tribute in the same way. The emperor gave up his journey to Rome and came to Noviomagus.
The emperor held his inquiry at Noviomagus. He asked why the coast was not defended. The great men said: because the Frisians would not obey us.
So there is to be a fleet. And until there is a fleet there is the tribute. Every house that trades on the dams is set down for its part.
Pay your house's part of the tribute, 25 d
Give 25 d toward the emperor's ships instead
Say you were at sea, and your silver with you
The emperor's hall at Noviomagus above the Waal, grey-bearded Louis seated among counts and bishops, a clerk reading names from a roll; rain at the open door.
The sea over Frisia

On the day after Christmas, the feast of Saint Stephen, a great flood broke over Frisia against the way of the tides and covered almost the whole land. The drowned were counted with care: two thousand four hundred and thirty-seven.
The water stood level with the dunes. Men, cattle and houses went out with it together. On the mounds they stood in the dark and listened.
Someone counted the dead to the last child. I do not know who. I would like to meet a man who can count like that and still sleep.
The mound country has no cattle, no cheese and no seed corn this year. It wants grain and timber, and will pay in what silver the sea left.
Take an order for corn
Take an order for oak, to raise the houses again
Give 20 d for the burying of the dead
A terp village standing as an island in brown water under a winter moon, people and a few cattle crowded on the mound, a church roof and a drifting haystack; a priest with a lantern.
Three kings
The emperor Louis is dead, and his sons have fought each other at Fontenoy with a slaughter such as no man remembers among the Franks. The coasts are left to whoever comes.
Lothar has given Walichrum to Harald the Dane, to hold against the other Danes. Christian people handed to a heathen. Men say it is a deed to be detested, and they say it quietly.
In Saxony the common men have risen for the law of their heathen fathers. Stellinga, they call themselves. Lothar promised them that law if they would fight for him.
At Strasbourg the two younger kings swore to each other, each in the other's tongue, so the armies could follow it. Nobody has yet sworn anything to a merchant.
It is settled at Verdun. Charles has the west, Louis the east, and Lothar the middle, with Frisia, the Rhine mouths and the Maas. Three kings. Three tolls.
Pay the clerk to write you a letter of protection in Lothar's name (20 d)
Carry the clerk's letters down the river for him
Trust no king's parchment this year, and keep your silver on you
A clerk at a writing board in a toll house by a river, three small wax seals laid in a row before him, armed riders passing the open door in dust; high summer.
Quentovic at dawn

This year a fleet of the Northmen came to the trading place called Quentovic at first light, plundered it, took captives, killed people of both sexes, and left nothing in it but the houses that were bought off with a price.
I paid. So my house stands, in a street of ash, and my neighbours' widows look at it. I am not sure it was the better bargain.
From there they crossed and did the same at Hamwic. The crossing is no shorter for them than for us. They only do not pay the toll.
Buy his wine at his price: he needs silver more than casks (two for 80 d)
Lend him 40 d to buy back his neighbours' roof-timber
Hear him, and say what one says
A street of burned house-plots at grey dawn with one whole timber house standing in it, a well-dressed merchant in its doorway, women in the ash looking toward him.
Silver from Quentovic
A boy off a Channel boat has been asking for you by name. He carries a sealed purse from the wine merchant of Quentovic, and half of a split tally stick.
Inside are your forty pennies, counted, and a word by the boy's mouth: that the street has roofs again, and that there is a cask put by for your house every vintage while he lives.
Match the tally, take the silver, and send for the cask
Take the silver and send the cask's worth back for the widows
A boy in a salt-stained cloak on a quay holding out a sealed leather purse and half a notched tally stick; a Channel boat unloading casks behind him; clear windy day.
Seven thousand pounds

This year Ragnar went up the Seine with a hundred and twenty ships and came to Parisius at Easter. King Charles gave him seven thousand pounds of silver to go away. In the same year the Danes burned Hamburg. The men are home, and selling.
A cup. A book cover with stones in it. A little silver house that had bones in it. I threw out the bones. What will you give?
Many died on the way home, of a sickness in the belly. The Christians say their saint did it. Then the saint should have done it before we reached his church.
Church plate may not be bought or sold among Christians. Brought home to its church, it is another matter.
Buy the cup, to carry it back to a church (60 d)
Buy his ordinary loot instead: a bundle of silk trim for 30 d
Buy nothing that came out of a church

A raider home from the Seine squatting on a northern beach with church silver spread on a cloak: a chalice, a jewelled book cover, an empty house-shaped shrine; ships drawn up behind, midsummer evening.
The cup comes home
You carry a chalice bought off a raider's cloak in the north. A priest on the quay has seen its shape through the wrapping.
That was made for an altar. I will not ask how you came by it. I will ask where it is going.
By the law no man buys or sells such a thing. A man may bring one back.
Give it to his church, and take his prayers
Give it, and ask the sixty pennies it cost you
Say it is a cup, and yours
A priest in a church porch unwrapping a silver chalice from a merchant's cloak and turning it to the light, the merchant standing with his cap in his hand; low morning sun through the door.
The emperor watches

This year the Northmen burned Dorestat with two other villages, in the sight of the emperor Lothar, who lay in the stronghold at Noviomagus and could not punish the deed. They went home with their ships full, and Frisia paid tribute.
From the hall at Noviomagus you can see a long way down the river. He had the best view of any man in the realm.
Each time it burns, the dams are built again a little shorter. The men who built them the first time are dead, or at Traiectum.
The man you paid to watch the river mouth sent word a day ahead. Your people had the goods upriver before the sails showed.
Send 40 d for timber to mend your jetty
Take a place on the bank at Daventre on the IJssel, while there is time (60 d)
Do nothing yet. It has been built again before
A stone-footed hall high above a broad river, a crowned man at a window looking down the valley toward a far column of smoke; afternoon haze.
Rorik the Dane holds Dorestat for the emperor. His men take the king's tenth and nothing over, and pay well for wine and for news of other fleets.
A Dane holds Dorestat

This year Rorik the Dane came by the mouths of the Rhine with a fleet and took Dorestat. The emperor Lothar could not drive him out, so he received him as his man and gave him Dorestat and other counties, to pay the king's dues and keep off the other Danes.
He takes the tenth like any count. He hangs thieves like any count. The difference is that the other Danes know him, and know what he does to them.
The toll man at Dorestat is a Dane now. He weighs fairly. He does not like to be argued with.
Send Rorik's toll man a gift by this skipper, so your name is known (15 d)
Keep your goods out of a heathen's county, and trade by Traiectum
Ask the Dane what Rorik's men buy
A Danish lord in a Frankish cloak seated on the toll house step at Dorestat, a Frankish clerk beside him with tally sticks, longships and merchant boats moored together along the dam; clear morning.
A church at Sliesthorp
King Horik has let Bishop Anskar build a church at Sliesthorp, the port where merchants come from every side, and has given leave to any in his kingdom to become Christian who will.
Before it stood, the traders from Dorestat and Hamburg were afraid to come here. Now they come freely, and the place has more of everything.

Many here were baptised at Dorestat or Hamburg already. Others take the sign of the cross, so they may come into the church, and put off the water until they are dying. They think it washes more that way.
We have no bell. The heathen hold a bell to be a thing forbidden. I find the quiet worse.
Take the priest's order for Mass wine
Give 10 d to the church
Wish him well, and mind your trade
A small new timber church by a northern harbour among turf-roofed booths, a tonsured priest at its door speaking with a Frisian merchant, heathen traders looking on; long evening light.
While Rorik was away

This year Rorik took his fleet to the borders of the Danes and seized the land between the sea and the Eider. While he was gone, other Danes stormed Dorestat and laid waste the Betuwe, and Saint Martin's at Traiectum was destroyed. Bishop Hunger has fled with his clergy.
We carried the books and the bones. The bishop is lame and was carried also. The king has promised us a roof far up the Maas. Some talk of Daventre.
A Dane was set to keep the Danes out. He did, while he was there.
Give the brothers passage up the river
Buy a book they can no longer carry (120 d)
Give them 4 d for bread and ale on the road
Stand aside and let them pass
A line of monks on a river bank in rain carrying book-chests and a reliquary on poles, a lame bishop in a litter, smoke behind them over a church tower.
The last of Dorestat

In the winter of this year, when the rivers were in flood, the Danes came up the Rhine and plundered Dorestat, and a large homestead besides where the Frisian merchants had fled. They killed many of the merchants, took a multitude captive, and went on toward Colonia.
We thought the big farm was safe. All the merchants thought so, which is why they were all in it.
They left by the road they came, on Rorik's advice, they say. Whose advice they came by, nobody says.
Your house's name was known to Rorik's toll man. It did not help the men in the farmhouse.
Nobody speaks of building the dams again.
Send 50 d toward the ransom of the merchants taken
Take him on: a merchant's son who can reckon
Let the dead bury the dead, and look for another harbour
A flooded winter river plain with a great timber farmstead burning on its mound, longships nosed into the flood among drowned willows, captives roped on the bank; iron-grey sky.
The river has gone elsewhere
The Rhine no longer runs as it did. Year by year the stream goes south by the Lek and the Waal, and the old arm past Dorestat lies shallow and choked with sand. A laden boat cannot come to the dams.
My father poled across in ten strokes with water over the pole. I walk it in August. A river is like a buyer. It goes where the way is easier.
The men who are left carry their goods to Tiel on the Waal, or up the IJssel to Daventre. The bishop's men have gone to Daventre already. Dorestat they have begun to call the Wik.
Your house has had a place on the bank at Daventre since Lothar's day.
Go to the place your house took at Daventre
Move the house to Daventre: a place on the IJssel bank, 80 d
Go with the others to Tiel on the Waal
Stay by the old dams, and trade in what small boats can carry
A long row of rotting jetties standing over dry sand and reeds, a ferryman walking where the river was, one small boat aground; far off, sails moving on another river; hot still noon.
The edict of Pîtres

This year at Pîtres on the Seine King Charles ordered that whoever gives or sells a mail coat, arms or a horse to the Northmen, for ransom or any price, shall lose his life as a traitor to his country. He ordered also a new penny, from ten mints and no more.
No fine and no appeal. A horse, a sword, a mail coat: it is your neck. The king had it written so that nobody could say he had not heard.
The old pennies pass until Martinmas. After that they are bad coin. And a man who refuses a good new one is flogged, or fined if he is free.
I see what you carry. Inside the realm it is trade. Think carefully about where the realm ends.
Sell a sword here, to a Frank, for what it fetches
Change your old pennies before Martinmas
Hear the law, and say you have heard it

A royal officer reading from a parchment on the steps of a market cross by the Seine, a new timber bridge-fort behind him, horse dealers and merchants listening, a bright new penny held up between two fingers; midsummer.
A great army
This year a great heathen army came into the land of the English and took winter quarters among the East Angles. There they were given horses, and the East Angles made peace with them.
Not a fleet that comes for the summer. An army, with its own kings, that does not mean to go home. They asked for horses and got them.
What do you sell to an army? Everything. Once. Then it owns the place where you bought it.
An army in winter quarters wants ale, bread, cloth and iron, and pays in other men's silver.
Send word to Gipeswic that you will bring ale and cloth for the camp
Call in what you are owed among the East Angles before the army spends it
Keep out of English waters until it is seen who rules there
A winter camp of hundreds of tents and ships drawn up along an East Anglian river, farmers leading a string of horses toward it under guard; frost and low sun.
Eoforwic

This year the army went from the East Angles over the mouth of the Humber to Eoforwic. The Northumbrians had cast out their king Osberht and taken another, Ælla. Late in the year the two made peace and came against the army together, and both kings were killed.
They took the city on All Saints' day. Two kings quarrelling over a house while a stranger moved in.
On the Friday before Palm Sunday our two kings broke in over the old wall together. That was the last thing either of them did.
The mint and the market of Eoforwic are the Danes' now. They weigh silver and care little whose head is on it.
The blood owed at Eoforwic since the old Frisian quarrel has no one left to claim it.
Send word to Eoforwic that a Frisian boat will come to the new masters
Buy his black jet at his price, for he must eat (two sacks, 30 d)
Leave Northumbria to the Northumbrians and the Danes
The broken Roman wall of York in March rain, Danish shields along the top, two crowned bodies carried out through a gap on shields; small figures under a wide grey sky.
The saint on the road

This year the army under Halfdan wintered on the Tyne and wasted the land. Bishop Eardulf and the people of Saint Cuthbert left the holy island with the saint's body in its coffin, and they carry it from place to place with no house to set it down in.
Seven of us bear him. We have his body, King Oswald's head, and the great gospel book. We have no roof. He never cared much for roofs, in life.
We thought to cross to Ireland with him. The sea stood up against the ship, and the book went over the side. It lay on the sand at the next ebb, hardly marked. I do not ask you to believe it.
Give 20 d to the saint's people
Carry their baggage by sea to the next river mouth
Uncover your head as the coffin passes, and go on
Seven men carrying a wooden coffin on poles along a northern shore at low tide, a bishop walking before with a book wrapped in cloth, gulls and a long wet strand; pale light.
The heathen army holds Chippenham and has overrun the West Saxons. King Alfred is in the marshes of Somerset with a small band. Many have fled over the sea.
The king in the marsh

This year, at midwinter after Twelfth Night, the army stole away to Chippenham and rode over the land of the West Saxons and sat down in it. Many of the people they drove over the sea. King Alfred with a small band went into the woods and the fastnesses of the moors.
My husband went into the marsh with the king. I went over the sea with the children. One of us chose badly, and I do not yet know which.
I have a ring. I need bread, and a roof till the cuckoo sings.
Lend her 30 d on the ring, to be redeemed
Give her 10 d and ask nothing
Ask her what is left of Wessex
A West Saxon woman with two children on a Frankish quay in February sleet, a bundle at her feet, holding out a gold ring on her open palm to a merchant.
The ring redeemed

In the seventh week after Easter King Alfred rode to Edington and fought the whole army and put it to flight. Guthrum their king was baptised with thirty of his men, and Alfred stood godfather to him. A West Saxon boy has been asking for your boat.
He has thirty pennies in a knotted cloth, and ten more, and a message: that the lady's husband came out of the marsh alive, and that there is a welcome for your boat at Hamwic.
Take the forty and give back the ring
Take the thirty you lent, and send the ten back
A boy in a West Saxon cloak on a sunny quay holding out a knotted cloth of pennies; behind him a ship making ready for England.
Alfred's and Guthrum's peace

King Alfred and King Guthrum have sworn a peace and drawn a line: up the Thames, up the Lea to its source, straight to Bedford, and up the Ouse to Watling Street. No man goes over to the army without leave. Those who must cross to trade give hostages for their good faith.
An Englishman and a Dane are worth the same now, dead: eight half-marks of pure gold. Alive, each stays on his own side unless I say so.
You want to sell on the Danes' side. Then I want a pledge that you come back with a clean name. A man of yours, or silver in my chest.
Leave silver in the reeve's chest as your pledge: he keeps 4 d for the keeping
Leave one of your men with him until you come back
Sell on this side of the line, and keep your men and your silver
An English reeve at a river ford with a chest at his feet and a peeled boundary stake behind him, a Frisian merchant counting pennies into his hand, Danes waiting on the far bank; overcast afternoon.
Horses in the emperor's chapel

This winter the Northmen sat in a camp at Elsloo on the Maas and burned Liège, Maastricht, Colonia and Bonn. At Aachen they stabled their horses in the chapel of the great Charles. In the summer the emperor came against them with a great host, and then paid them.
Colonia had walls from the Romans and nobody on them. I got out by the river with what the boat would hold.
Godfrid was washed in the font and given Frisia, all that Rorik held. Sigfrid was given silver by the thousand pound. The host went home. I am told this is a victory.
Now they have burned Daventre too, the port on the IJssel where Saint Lebuin lies, and killed many.
The wine of the Rhine has no road north this year.
Buy his wine: three casks for 120 d
Give 20 d toward walls for the river towns
Count yourself lucky to trade on salt water
The round chapel at Aachen in winter with horses tethered between its columns and straw on the marble floor, Northmen at a fire in the doorway, snow blowing in.
The Dane's county ends

This year Godfrid the Northman, who held Frisia from the emperor, asked for Coblenz, Andernach and Sinzig besides, for the sake of their wine. He was called to a meeting at Herispich in the Betuwe and killed there by the emperor's men.
He wanted the wine lands, because his own county grows none. They gave him an island to talk on, and a sword to end the talk.
So there is no Danish count in Frisia. There is, for the moment, no count at all. The toll is being taken by whoever stands nearest the rope.
Pay whoever holds the rope: 6 d
Ask to see whose man he is
Lie off until a count is named
A river island in the Betuwe with two parties of armed men facing each other under willows, one man falling; boats waiting on both banks; midsummer noon.
King Alfred has set Lunden in order. The market moves inside the Roman walls, with plots along the hithe, under Æthelred the ealdorman.
Lundenburh

This year King Alfred set Lunden in order again, and all the English who were not under the Danes turned to him. He gave the town into the keeping of Æthelred the ealdorman. The market is moving from the old strand into the Roman walls.
The wic on the strand is nettles. Inside the walls they are laying out streets from the river to the market, and plots along the hithe for those who come first.
The ealdorman wants ships to come. A hithe with no ships is a wall with a hole in it.
Send 40 d by a sure hand as earnest for a place at the new hithe
Ask what the toll will be inside the walls
Wait and see whether the walls hold
The Roman river wall of London seen from the Thames at high water, men pegging out plots with cord between the wall and a beach where one ship is drawn up; clear cold morning.
What Ohthere told the king

A Northman named Ohthere has told King Alfred how he lives northmost of all the Northmen, how he sailed north round the land until it bent south again, and how many days' sail it is from his home to the Danes' port. A clerk of the king's household has it written down.
He brought the king walrus teeth. He counts his wealth in tame deer, and in what the Finns pay him: skins, bird-down, whale-bone, and ship-rope of walrus hide.
Another, Wulfstan, told of seven days and nights under sail from the Danes' port east to Truso, and of the Este, who keep their dead unburied a month and ride races for the goods.
Pay for a copy of Ohthere's sailing (10 d)
Pay for a copy of Wulfstan's (10 d)
Listen while he reads, and keep what you can in your head
A clerk at a slanted desk in a king's hall reading from a fresh leaf, a tall Northman with a walrus tusk under his arm standing before a seated king behind him; firelight.
The king's long ships

This year King Alfred had long ships built against the raiders, near twice as long as theirs, some of sixty oars and some of more: swifter, steadier and higher, shaped neither like the Frisian nor like the Danish, but as he thought most useful. There were Frisians among the crews.
Nine of them caught six Danes in a river mouth on the south coast. Then the tide went out and left the king's ships on the wrong bank. A ship so long is very steady, aground.
Wulfheard the Frisian died there, and Æbbe the Frisian, and Æthelhere the Frisian. Sixty-two of ours, Frisians and English together. I was fourth from the bow and am fairly alive.
The king pays his shipmen in silver, by the season. I have had a season of it.
Take him on: he has rowed in a king's ship and lived
Buy him ale and hear the fight told properly (2 d)
A man who has taken a king's pay will not like a merchant's
Very long warships lying aground on a mudbank at low tide with men fighting between them in the shallows, smaller Danish ships beginning to float off; grey estuary, far shore.
The freedom that was Dorestat's
This year King Zwentibold confirmed to the church of Traiectum that its men who live at Daventre and at Tiel shall have the same freedom from the king's toll that they had at Dorestat.
The charter says: as they had in Dorestat. It does not say that Dorestat is gone. Charters are polite.

If your house is the bishop's man, the freedom is yours where the bishop's men now sit. If your house held a freedom of its own at Dorestat, bring the parchment. I will see what can still be read of it.
Show the old Dorestat freedom, and have it written over to Daventre
Become the bishop's man for the toll's sake: 120 d and a candle every year
Go on paying the toll like a free man
A bishop's clerk unrolling a new sealed charter on a barrel head at a river landing, a merchant holding an old cracked parchment beside it; boats from the Waal behind; summer afternoon.
Rollo the Northman holds Rotomagus from the king and is baptised. The Seine is shut to other raiders. His men buy wine, weapons and good cloth, and sell what their fathers took.
A Northman at Rotomagus
King Charles has given the city of Rotomagus and the land about the mouth of the Seine to Rollo and his Northmen, to hold against other Northmen. Rollo has been baptised.
He was washed white on the Sunday and gave land to seven churches in seven days. On the eighth he shared out the rest among his men with a rope.
A plough can be left in the field overnight now. He hangs thieves, and those who hide thieves. The river is shut to every raider but him.
They tell it that when he was to kiss the king's foot he had one of his men do it, who lifted the foot to his mouth and tipped the king over. I was not there. Nobody was there. Everybody tells it.
Send word to Rotomagus that you will bring Rhine wine
Ask what the Northmen at Rotomagus buy
A wolf in a white robe. Leave the Seine a few years yet
A broad-shouldered Northman in a white baptismal robe standing in the door of the church at Rouen with a rope coiled over his arm, his men behind him, the Seine and moored ships below; autumn light.
Sliesthorp pays tribute
This year King Henry went with an army against the Danes, who were harrying the Frisians from the sea. He overcame them, made their king Gnupa pay tribute, and had him take baptism.
Gnupa's house came from the Svear and took the port in his father's day. Now the Saxon king's men stand by the Schlei as well. Two masters in one harbour, and both want the toll.
For us it is good. A Saxon can sell there under his own king's peace. For how long is another matter.
Take the Saxon king's peace: have your name set down with his man at Sliesthorp (30 d)
Keep your Danish host there, and pay his king's man as before
Send a small gift to each side and say little (12 d)
A Danish king kneeling at a wooden font held by a Saxon bishop on the shore of the Schlei, Saxon horsemen in a half ring, the curved harbour palisade and ships behind; flat summer light.
The hot iron

King Harald, Gorm's son, has taken baptism and ordered the Danes to be Christian. It is told that at a feast the Danes held Christ to be a god, but others greater; and that a priest named Poppo carried a great weight of glowing iron in his hand and showed it unharmed.
I did not see the iron. I have seen the churches going up since, which is the greater wonder, because Danes are paying for them.
There have been bishops named for Sliesthorp, Ripa and Aarhus for half a man's life. Now some of them may even come.
A church wants wine for the Mass, wax for the altar, a bell, and a book. This land grows none of them.
Take the order for wax and Mass wine
Give 15 d toward a bell
Notice that your Danish host still wears the hammer under his shirt, and say nothing
A priest holding up a bare unburned hand before a king and his feasting men in a long hall, a glowing iron bar lying on the hearth stones; firelight and smoke.
The emperor at the wall

This year the emperor Otto, the second of that name, came against the Danes, stormed the wall that guards their border at the gate called Wieglesdor, and built a stronghold in the march and set a garrison in it.
The wall was made to keep out Saxons. It has kept them out for a hundred and sixty winters, except when they came.
The road south through the gate is shut this season. What used to go by cart to the Eider waits on the quay, and gets cheaper.
Your house has stood under the Saxon king's peace at Sliesthorp since Gnupa's day. This year that is the safe side.
Your house kept its Danish host at Sliesthorp. This year he is on the losing side, and will remember who stood by him.
Send 60 d for marten from what waits on the quay
Send your Danish host a gift in his bad year (20 d)
Keep out of a harbour with an army at its gate
Mailed German riders pouring through a timber gate in a long earth wall across heath, Danish defenders falling back, the emperor's banner; hot dusty afternoon.
The Danes take back the march

This year the Danes fell on the stronghold the emperor had built in their march, took it by craft, and burned it. In the same summer the Slavs beyond the Elbe rose, destroyed the bishops' seats at Havelberg and Brandenburg, and burned Hamburg.
The emperor was in Italy, losing to the Saracens. Everybody north of the Elbe heard that before his own counts did.
The Saxon booths at Sliesthorp are empty. Mine is. A Dane has the keys of it, and I have the tally of what was in it.
Your house took the Saxon peace there in Gnupa's day. The Danes have long memories, and a new king's man.
Your Danish host at Sliesthorp has not forgotten your house. Your booth is where you left it.
Send the Danish king's man 40 d and call it harbour dues for the lost years
Buy the Saxon's tally: his goods at Sliesthorp are yours if your host can find them (50 d)
Let Saxons and Danes settle it between them
A timber stronghold burning at night on a heath beside a long earth wall, Danes with torches, a few Saxon traders with packs slipping away along the shore of the fjord.
One coin, and witnesses

By the king's law there is one coinage over all his dominion, and no man strikes it except in a town. Nothing worth more than twenty pennies is to be bought outside a town, but inside, before the reeve or other trusty men.
Twenty pennies. Above that you buy inside the port and I see it done. On the beach you may buy a hen.

King Edgar's new penny is the only penny. Old ones and foreign ones go to the moneyer, and he gives you new, less his due. In a few years there will be a newer one. Kings have found out what moneyers always knew.
A moneyer who strikes false loses the hand he did it with, and it is set up over his workshop. So you may trust the coin.
Buy and sell inside the port, before his witnesses
Do your larger business on the beach beyond the stakes
Take your foreign silver to the moneyer now
An English reeve and two witnesses standing over a sale of cloth at a market stall inside a town gate, a severed hand nailed above a moneyer's shuttered workshop behind them; plain daylight.
Birka on its island is given up. The king of the Svear has laid out a new town, Sigtuna, on the north arm of the lake, and the trade goes there.
Birka lies empty

The town on the island in the lake of the Svear, where merchants came for two hundred winters, is given up. The king has had a new town marked out on the lake's north arm, in plots as even as the teeth of a comb, and calls it Sigtuna.
The channel my grandfather sailed, I have waded. The land comes up out of the water a hand's breadth in a man's life. A harbour will not wait for you.
And the silver from the east comes thinner. The men who went down the rivers go to the king's new town now, where he can see them.
Ask the way to the new town, and who gives out the plots
Buy what he brought out of Birka: a bundle of beaver and a string of beads, 45 d
Turn back for the Sound. The lake trade is for those who know it
An empty island town of grass-grown house plots and a rotting jetty standing above a shrunken shoreline, a hill fort behind, one small boat leaving; still summer evening on a lake.
The English have paid the fleet ten thousand pounds of silver to go away. The shipmen have English pennies to spend, and want wine, cloth and weapons.
Ten thousand pounds

This year Olaf came with ninety-three ships and harried the coast, and so to Maldon. Byrhtnoth the ealdorman fought him there and was killed. In that year it was first counselled to pay tribute to the Danish men, for the terror they made on the sea coast. That was at first ten thousand pounds.
Archbishop Sigeric gave the counsel. It is cheaper than an army. Everything is, the first time.
The old man let them cross the causeway to fight him on firm ground. Out of pride, the song says. I am a merchant. I would have let them stand in the mud.
Every thegn is set down for his part, and none of them has it in coin. They are selling land, cups and horses, and borrowing.
Lend a thegn 60 d against his harvest
Have the song of the fight written out for you (12 d)
Follow the silver: load what a paid fleet buys, and sell it where the ships winter
A tidal causeway in an Essex river at low water with two war-bands facing each other across it, a tall grey-haired ealdorman in the English front rank; August haze, ships beyond.
The thegn's harvest
The thegn who had your sixty pennies in the tribute year sends his reeve to you. The harvest was fair, and the king's men are asking for tribute again.
He can pay you in coin now and be short for the king, or in wool at the shearing price and keep his silver for the fleet.
Take the sixty pennies, counted
Take wool: ten sacks at his price
Take the sixty, and his word for your boat with the port reeve
An English estate reeve on a quay in autumn with a string of pack ponies carrying wool sacks, holding out a purse in one hand and pointing at the sacks with the other.
Saint Brice's day

This year the king ordered all the Danish men who were among the English to be slain on Saint Brice's mass-day, because it was told him that they would plot against his life and then have his kingdom. The reeve's men are going along the boats.
The king's word, to every port. At Oxford they fled into Saint Frideswide's, and the townsmen burned it over them, books and all. Who is aboard you?
I know a Frisian from a Dane. Mostly. Say each man's name, and where he was baptised.
One of your men was born on the far side of the sea and has never hidden it. He is sitting very still on the after thwart.
Say plainly that he is a Dane, your man, and leaving with you on this tide
Swear that every man aboard is a Frisian and a Christian
Put 30 d in the reeve's hand and say the tide is turning

A reeve and armed townsmen with torches on a November quay at dusk, looking down into a small trading boat where a fair-haired crewman sits rigid at the stern; smoke from a burning church beyond the roofs.
The hithe at Billingsgate

At Lunden the toll is set by the hull. A small ship pays a halfpenny at Billingsgate, a larger ship with sails a penny, a keel or a hulk fourpence if she lies there. The emperor's men, who come in their own ships, are held worthy of good laws like the townsmen.

Men of Rouen with wine or great fish pay six shillings for a large ship and a twentieth of the fish. Flanders, Ponthieu, Normandy and France show their goods and pay. Huy, Liège and Nivelles pay as they pass through.
The emperor's men give at Christmas and Easter: two grey cloths and a brown one, ten pounds of pepper, five pairs of gloves and two kegs of vinegar. You are from the Rhine mouth. Whose man are you?
Pay by the hull, like any ship
Say you are the emperor's man, and give a pound of pepper toward the Easter due
Unload nothing here, and go up to the next landing
The timber waterfront at Billingsgate with London's Roman wall behind, a reeve with tally sticks on the hithe, a Rhine ship unloading grey cloth and small sacks; a wet spring morning.
The great hunger

This year there was the great famine throughout the English, such that no man remembered one so grim. The fleet went back from this land to Denmark, and let but a little time pass before it came again.
The Danes left because there was nothing left to take. It is the first good the hunger has done.
There is silver here still. The king's moneyers never stop. A penny will not bake.
Promise corn: eight sacks within forty days
Sell two sacks from the hold at what they will give
Give a sack at the church door
An English churchyard in spring with thin people waiting at the door, new graves along the wall, a priest counting loaves out of a single basket; a merchant ship's mast showing above the roofs.
Tiel burned

This year Northmen came up the Waal with a great fleet. The people of Tiel fled, leaving all but their silver, and the port was plundered and burned, Saint Walburg's with it. At Traiectum the townsmen burned their own harbour quarter, so that the enemy should have no use of it.
We are merchants. We ran. The monks will say that we ran, and they will be right, and they were not there.
At Traiectum the townsmen had burned everything outside the wall themselves and stood on it. The Northmen said they wished no harm to the holy place, and went.
The men of Tiel trade with the English across the sea. Their stores are ash. Their debts are not.
Take an order for timber and tar for the rebuilding
Let him have 50 d until the English ships come
Shake your head with the rest
A river port on the Waal burning at dusk, long ships along the bank, townspeople streaming away over the dike with small heavy bags, a church tower alight.
A debt from Tiel
The merchant of Tiel who had fifty pennies of you after the fire has sold his English wool.
He sends the fifty by a boatman, and a cask of Rhine wine with a mark burned on the head that you do not know. The boatman says it is the mark the Tiel men use among themselves.
Take both, and send thanks
Take the silver, and send the cask back to be drunk in your house's name at their next feast
A river boatman rolling a wine cask up a plank onto a jetty, a brand mark on the cask head, a small purse tied to his belt; morning mist on the river.
The town's part of the tribute
The king and his counsellors have again promised the army tribute and food, if it will leave off its harrying. Every port is set down for its part, and the reeve has the roll.
Thirty-six thousand pounds, this time. Ten thousand, the first. They learn our prices quicker than we learn theirs.

Forty-eight thousand pounds this Easter. They held the archbishop at Greenwich. He would not let himself be ransomed, so they pelted him with ox bones at their feast, and one struck him down with the back of an axe. Then we paid.
Strangers who trade here pay with the town. It is your market too.
Pay your part with the town: 24 d
Say you are a stranger, and owe the English king nothing but his toll
Offer a bolt of cloth toward the army's food instead of coin
A reeve at a trestle on an English quay with a long parchment roll and a balance, townsmen in a line laying down pennies, cups and a silver cross; a Danish warship lying off in the river mist.
One king

This year King Æthelred died, and Edmund his son fought the army five times. At Assandun Cnut had the victory, and the flower of the English fell there. The kings met at Olney by Deerhurst and divided the land. On Saint Andrew's day King Edmund died, and Cnut took all the kingdom of the English.
The men of Lunden made their own peace with the army and bought it with silver, and the ships took winter quarters in the town.
A Dane is king from the Thames to the Sound. I have been afraid of Danish sails for thirty years. Now they are the king's ships, and I pay for them.
Send a gift to the new king's reeve at Lunden before the others think of it (40 d)
Load for both shores: wool for the Danes, amber for the English
Wait a year. Kings who come by the sword sometimes leave by it
Two kings clasping hands on a small river island in autumn, their armies on either bank, one king young and fair, the other wounded and leaning on a spear; mist on the Severn.
The fleet comes home rich

This year the tribute was paid over all the English: seventy-two thousand pounds, besides what the townsmen of Lunden paid, which was ten thousand five hundred. Some of the army went back to Denmark, and forty ships stayed with King Cnut.
I have a bag of English pennies with one king's face on every one. I want a sword with a name on it, wine, and a cloak my wife will not laugh at.
At Oxford the Danes and the English agreed to keep King Edgar's law. I do not know what it says. I know what it paid.
Take his order, and his neighbours'
Sell him a cask now, at a homecoming price
Look at his pennies, and tell him what they weigh

A Danish shipman home from England emptying a leather bag of silver pennies onto a ship's thwart in a Jutland harbour, his wife and neighbours watching, a merchant holding out a cup of wine to be tasted; bright cold day.
The count's toll on the Merwede

Count Dirk has built a stronghold at Vlaardingen in the marshes by the river mouth, and takes a heavy toll of the ships that pass. The merchants of Tiel complained to the emperor. This summer the emperor's host went down by ship to drive him out, and was cut to pieces among the ditches.
We told the emperor: if you do not protect us, we cannot cross to England, and the English cannot come to us, and then your own tolls will be the poorer. That, he understood.
The duke was taken, the bishops' men ran for the ships, and somebody shouted that all was lost before it was. Now the count keeps his fort, and his toll, and soon the emperor's pardon.
Reckon the count's toll into your prices, and sail by Vlaardingen
Go out by the Vecht and the Almere instead, the old way north, and lose three days
Put 20 d in the Tiel men's common purse for the next complaint
A wooden fort on a low mound among marsh ditches at a river mouth, armoured men floundering in the mud and running for ships, Frisians on the bank with spears; hot July noon.
The merchants of Tiel

The merchants of Tiel are hard men, used to no discipline. They judge cases not by the law but by their own will, and say the emperor has granted them this by charter. So a monk of the bishop's household tells it, who does not love them.
If one lends another a thing and the other denies it, he clears himself with an oath, and no witness at all. A man can swear a debt away while it is still in his fist.

They begin drinking at first light. He who tells foul tales loudest, and sets the simple folk laughing, has most praise. They gather money in common for it, and feast on the great days as if drunkenness were a solemn rite.
And they are the best payers the emperor's toll has.
The Tiel men know your house. A place would be made for it on the bench.
Take the place they offer your house on the bench
Pay into the common purse and drink with them for a season (40 d)
Agree with the monk, and give 10 d to Saint Walburg's
Watch how they settle a quarrel, and remember the oath they use
A long bench of red-faced merchants in a timber hall at first light, drinking horns and a shared money chest on the table, one man swearing with his hand raised, a thin monk watching from the door.
No more silver from the east

For as long as anyone remembers, silver came up the eastern rivers in round thin coins with writing on them that no one here could read. For some years now it has not come. The scales in the north weigh English and Saxon pennies instead.
My grandfather buried a chest of the eastern coins and died before he said where. My father looked for it till he died. I do not look. I have English pennies, from a king who paid us to go away.
Furs still go east. What comes back is cloth and beads. For silver a man goes west now, with goods or with an axe.
Buy his furs for western pennies: two timbers of squirrel for 30 d
Buy a folding scale and a set of his weights (8 d)
Ask where his grandfather's farm lay, and get no answer
A northern trader's folding scales on a sea-chest, a small heap of English pennies in one pan and lead weights in the other, an old cut dirham lying beside as a keepsake; lamp light.
The king's letter from Rome
This year King Cnut went to Rome and was at the hallowing of the emperor Conrad on Easter day. He has sent a letter home to all his people, and it is read in the churches.

He says: I spoke with the emperor, the pope and the princes of the needs of all my people, English and Danes: that they should have fairer law and safer peace on the road to Rome, and not be hindered by so many barriers, nor harassed with unjust tolls.
And the emperor agreed, and King Rudolf, who has most of those barriers in his hands. Merchants, and those who go to pray, are to go and come in firm peace, without barrier or toll-taker.
He had the pope ease what our archbishops pay for the pallium, too. A king who haggles for bishops and for pedlars in one breath.
The same was written once before, from one king to another, about pilgrims and black stones. Your house has the tale of it.
Offer passage to those who will go to Rome on the strength of it
Have the words about tolls written out, to show on the road (8 d)

One king, one toll, one peace from the Thames to the Sound, for a man's working life. Now three, and each will want ships.

Hedeby burned from end to end
This year Harald, king of the Northmen, at war with Sweyn of the Danes, came to the port by the Schlei that the Danes call Hedeby and the old annals Sliesthorp, and burned it from end to end.
One of his poets stood on the town wall before dawn and made a verse about the flames going up from the houses. A fine thing, to be burned by a man with a poet.

The long-haired star

This year at Easter-tide a sign was seen in the heavens such as no man had seen before. Some said it was the star called comet, which some call the long-haired star. It showed first on the eve of the Greater Litany, and shone all the week.

King Edward died on the eve of Twelfth Night, and Harold the earl was hallowed king the day after. The duke of the Normans says the kingdom was promised to him. The king of the Northmen says nothing, and builds ships.
The old men aboard remember no such star. One has heard that the like was seen in the old emperor Louis's day, and that Louis took it for his death and lived three years more.

Three fleets

All this summer King Harold has lain with ships and men by the Isle of Wight, waiting for the duke of the Normans. The duke lies with his ships at the mouth of the Somme, waiting for a south wind. And in the north Harald, king of the Northmen, is gathering three hundred ships.
Whoever has a hull is asked for it. Whoever has corn, ale, rope, tar or fodder is asked for that. Pay is promised on both shores, and on both shores it is the kingdom of England that is to pay it.
On the Nativity of Saint Mary the English king's food was gone, and no man could keep them there longer. The ships were sent up to Lunden, and many were lost before they came there.

The end of the old harbour
This year the Slavs beyond the Elbe killed their Christian prince Gottschalk at the altar and rose. They burned Hamburg, and fell on the rich town of the Danes on the Schlei and destroyed it utterly.

Two hundred and fifty winters it stood, since King Godfred set the merchants of Reric down on that shore. Burned by a Northman sixteen years ago, by the Wends this year. A third time it will not be built.

King Harold killed the king of the Northmen at Stamford Bridge, and nineteen days later was killed himself, fighting the duke of the Normans near Hastings. The English have no king.
Two battles

This year Harald, king of the Northmen, came into the Humber with three hundred ships. King Harold came on him unawares at Stamford Bridge, and the Northman was killed there. Then the duke of the Normans landed in the south. King Harold marched against him and fell, on Saint Calixtus's day, and his two brothers with him.
We went the length of England twice in three weeks, on foot. We won the first fight. I would like that remembered.
One Northman held the bridge alone until somebody went under it in a boat with a spear. Every army has one such man. At the second fight we did not have him, or we had him and he was tired.
Of the three hundred ships that came into the Humber, twenty-four were enough to carry home those who were left.

Midwinter

The duke of the Normans has been received at Berkhamsted by the archbishop, the child Edgar, the earls and the best men of Lunden. They gave hostages and swore oaths to him. On midwinter's day he is hallowed king at Westminster.
